items.title: One authority per fact; every durable decision has exactly one home
items.ezx: Every fact and every lasting decision lives in exactly one file, so copies can never drift apart. A triage rule sorts each decision into one of four homes: the design model, an architecture decision record, a contract row, or the code with its tests.

content nature to exactly one of four homes — model (admission test K0), ADR

items.title: A rule without an enforcement surface is a planning gap, and a decision record without a verification clause is prose
items.ezx: A binding rule that nothing enforces is treated as a hole in the plan, not as a rule. Likewise, a recorded decision must say how to check that it is still being followed — otherwise it is just prose.
items.original:
Every binding `IC-*` constraint maps to a test, a check, or an ADR ("An item
with none of the three is a planning gap"), every `PI-*` item has a home in
the plan, and every ADR's `Verification` section is mandatory ("an ADR
without a way to check it is still in force is prose, not a contract").

items.title: Push constraints down the ladder: environment > data > in-context rule
items.ezx: A constraint enforced by the environment — types, schemas, linters, fixtures — costs nothing to remember and fails locally, so it beats a rule written as text an AI must keep in mind. When a rule is needed, the order of preference is: mechanize it, extend an existing reviewer duty, and only as a last resort write new prose.
items.original:
A constraint the environment enforces (types, schema, lint, fixtures) costs
zero context and fails locally; data (the finished artifact) beats prose
rules; the in-context budget is the scarce resource, and the admission bias
prefers "mechanize → extend an existing lens duty → new prose rule".

items.title: Evidence over claims; "driven" means able to fail
items.ezx: A claim that something is complete or was swept only counts when it comes with the actual, untruncated measurement output — a list recalled from memory is not a measurement. A test only counts if it is proven able to fail when the thing it guards is broken.

A completeness or sweep claim is admissible only with its untruncated
measurement ("enumeration from memory is not a measurement"); a gate's
negative test derives from its DECLARED claim, never from the implemented
rule list; a test lane counts only when it can catch a violation of its
row's meaning ("'Driven' means ABLE TO FAIL … presence is not sensitivity").

items.title: The process governs its own changes
items.ezx: The documents that define the process are put through the same machinery as ordinary work: multiple review rounds, an outside reviewer, explicit human ratification, and the process's own rules applied to itself. No document anywhere states this as a rule — it is visible only in how the process documents were actually produced.
items.original:
*Practiced, not recorded.* Process-defining documents are themselves run
through the process's adversarial machinery rather than written by fiat:
`v3/implementation/process-v2-design.md` went through six review rounds and
applies its own D2 one-authority rule to itself; the autonomy realignment was

authority rewrites go through the claim-enumeration ritual (M13) before the
prose is written. No surface states "process changes obey the process" as a
principle — it is inferable only from how the process documents were
produced, which is what makes it a genuine institutionalization datum rather
than a quoted rule. Its written cousins exist but are narrower: P9 governs
WHEN the process may change (boundaries only), P11 governs WHAT may be
admitted; neither says the change itself must be reviewed and ratified like
work.

items.title: Chapter-based plan progression
items.ezx: The plan is written and executed one chapter at a time: each chapter is proposed, then explicitly approved by the human, then committed — there is no single big up-front plan. Approval freezes the chapter's table of work items, execution modes, and pre-registered predictions.
items.original:
The plan is written and executed chapter by chapter, "each chapter proposed
→ ratified → committed. No monolithic draft"; new chapters append via the
§1.3 map-extension mechanism with an explicit build-order slot (ch11–ch13
entered this way), and ratification fixes the packet table, flow modes,
pre-registered predictions, and (under experiment 2) the chapter's
main-thread model.

items.title: The packet build loop
items.ezx: Every planned step runs the same fixed cycle: write the packet (the self-contained work-order document), read the sources, write tests first, implement, get the drift tests green, record a decision if one was made, review, commit once, then audit. A packet decision that contradicts the ratified plan must be folded up into the plan in the same commit, never silently and never later.
items.original:
Every plan step runs the same fixed cycle (steps 0–8): author the packet →
read the spec + ledger slice → TDD from declared claims → implement → drift
tests green → ADR if a trigger fires → review (code + ADR compliance) →
one-step-one-commit → post-build audit; a red audit "is a defect fixed
before any further packet work, never advisory". A packet decision
contradicting ratified plan text flows UP into the plan "IN THE SAME COMMIT,
marked 'aligned at <packet-id> pre-approval'. Never silent, never deferred"
(R-ALIGNED-UP).

The one-packet-one-commit rule carries NAMED exception classes, not
judgment calls. The plan's own §14.4 text at this head names ONE — the
schema re-lock follow-up commit, which cannot ride the build commit because
its re-lock block records that commit's own sha. A SECOND is defined and
confined in `v3/implementation/task-packet-template.md`: the
INSTRUMENT-LANDING commit, where a packet whose acceptance proof needs a
baseline recomputable at a pre-change ref lands its measuring instrument in
the build commit's PARENT, declared by content in the opt-in
`instrument_manifest` block (exact keyset, nonempty, unique, repo-relative,
every path under `v3/src/testkit/`) and audited by its own lint leg. The two
surfaces disagree at this head: the template calls the instrument landing
"the plan §14.4 SECOND named exception" while §14.4 itself still says "ONE"
— the plan-side text was written but is uncommitted at this head
(2026-08-18 arm finding #3, the ledger's own review-basis lesson).
sources: v3/implementation/task-packet-template.md (the `instrument_manifest` block — the second commit exception's confinement)

items.title: The five-lens fresh-context review panel
items.ezx: Every packet and draft is reviewed by five sub-agents with no prior context, each looking through a different lens, sharing one verdict vocabulary: split, refine, or approve. Approval is tied to the exact final content hash — any later content change voids it — and before any approve, an audit verifies that every required output actually exists in the target document.
items.original:
One review engine for packets and drafts: five fresh-context sub-agent
lenses with a Gate Coverage Matrix and one verdict set
(`split`/`refine`/`approve` + STOP); first round FULL, content folds trigger
TARGETED re-runs with mandatory escalation triggers, bookkeeping folds get
one reconciliation pass, and the approve requires a clean top-level
reconciliation close bound to the final content hash ("any later CONTENT
fold voids it"); includes the once-per-packet fresh-implementer lens
experiment. Before any approve, the Mandatory Output Audit verifies every
triggered mandatory output is MATERIALIZED in the target (adjacent prose may
not substitute); the finding policy is fix-by-default because "the fresh
reviewer is a proxy for the build-time implementer", and the spec-vs-build
altitude line routes fixture-level demands to `deferred-to-build` by rule.

items.title: The contract-drafting ritual (DraftContract)
items.ezx: A chapter's design decisions are frozen once as numbered contract rows, panel-reviewed, then ratified by the human in a two-commit ceremony that records the date, the reviewers, and the commit. Reopening a ratified contract is a deliberate, loudly-marked exception window, and the human sign-off itself is never automated.
items.original:
A chapter's memo-born surface is decided once as `C<n>` rows,
panel-reviewed, then human-ratified via a two-commit act (content commit at
`draft`, ratifying commit appending `{date, arms, commit}` and flipping to
`ratified`); packets anchor as `contract:chN-<surface>#Cn`; reopen is a
deliberate loud-red two-commit window, and chapter close fills the
`realized_map` and flips to `realized` in one act.
`tools/v3-plan/reopen_runner.py` executes the file operations of a reopen —
"the human ratification act stays human".
sources: v3/implementation/contracts/ (7 drafts: ch8, ch9, ch11, ch12, ch13, ch13-v2, ch14)

items.title: External-arm invocation
items.ezx: For an outside opinion, a different AI model — pinned to an exact version per chapter — reviews the exact target bytes, under a guard that proves the bytes did not change during the review. Since August 2026 the main route runs the outside model as an agent, with the older wrapper script kept as the portable fallback; on the agent route the same guards are performed by hand. A record may name which model tier ran only when a machine confirmed it.
items.original:
A different model (pinned per chapter in `v3/implementation/arm-pin.md` —
currently an external reviewer model at high reasoning effort) reviews target bytes under a byte guard.
TRANSPORT (user ruling 2026-08-10, pin row landed at the ch13 boundary
2026-08-14): the PRIMARY transport is the external reviewer agent — model and effort
pinned in the agent definition, and the guards reproduced BY HAND on that
route (basis-hash check before and after the run; provenance — transport ·
model · effort · timestamps — in the verdict header). The FALLBACK is
`tools/v3-plan/arm_run.sh`, which carries the same guards mechanically:
availability preflight, pin match read from the pin table's last row,
foreground launch under a 45-minute timeout (recalibrated from 20 after the
cap killed four actively-working runs), header-pin validation, and
before/after byte-guard; exits `2 usage/preflight · 3 pin-mismatch · 4
guard-trip · 5 arm-error · 6 guard-infra`. The asymmetry between the two
routes is recorded rather than papered over: the primary transport carries no
runner-side timeout, and "a requested-vs-actual assertion is not buildable on
the agent transport today" — the call must also not pass a model parameter,
since one `model:` override invalidated a run as a pin mismatch. TIER-RECORD
RULE (same boundary, born from a tier-mismatched ratification
review the owner caught at the gate): a record names a MODEL TIER only when
the tier is MACHINE-CONFIRMED (a pin-validated header, or a transport that
reports its model); otherwise it names the REQUEST and the uncertainty, and
"a silent tier claim is the named defect".

items.title: Friction capture and the chapter boundary review
items.ezx: Observations about the process are appended to a log the moment they happen; at each chapter boundary every new line gets a verdict — become a gate, become a rule, edit the docs, watch it, or acknowledge it as a non-issue. A tally of how often each standing rule actually caught something feeds the retirement sweep, and one-off observations default to "watch".
items.original:
Observations are appended to the process log the moment they happen; at each
chapter boundary every new line gets a verdict (gate / checkpoint rule /
README edit / WATCH / acknowledged non-issue), `later-chapter` verdicts land
their plan-map rows in the same act, a per-rule catch tally feeds the
retirement sweep, and single-occurrence candidates default to WATCH. The
boundary is also where the autonomy machinery is measured and where two
standing settings may move: autonomously-approved packets are post-hoc
audited for `detector_misses` — "a miss is a DETECTOR bug: fix the rule, do
not add process", and the boundary "evaluates the gates' yield from the
`detector_misses` stream" (`v3/implementation/README.md` §5.5, §7) — and the
external-arm pin is revisable at chapter boundaries ONLY. A boundary verdict
can also close a running pilot on its own recorded data (the ch13 boundary,
2026-08-14, stopped the mutation-testing pilot — see U2).

items.title: Fresh-context delegated build (the conductor architecture) with the entry-mode trust dial
items.ezx: By default the actual build work is handed to a fresh sub-agent that receives only the self-contained packet, while the main session keeps orchestration, the verification chain, and the commit boundary. The user's opening prompt sets how far the loop may run unattended.
items.original:
The default build is a subagent fed the self-contained packet executing
steps 1–3, while the main context keeps orchestration, the verification
chain, both arm gates, and the commit boundary; delegation prompts must
QUOTE any discipline stronger than the existing suite; under standing
chapter mode "every heavy step — authoring, build, arm runs — delegates to
fresh-context subagents". The user's opening prompt sets how far the loop
runs unattended: bare "go ahead with chN-pM" = PER-PACKET (flag-free ⇒ autonomous
through build, announced in one line, stop after the packet); "review chN-pM"
= stop at the approve; "delegate chapter chN" = STANDING chapter mode,
valid only under the conductor architecture. A per-item token overrides a
standing mode, and an undetermined mode on a flag-free approve resolves to
the letter WITH the announcement — "never a silent discretionary stop"
(`AGENTS.md`, V3 Implementation Plane).

SUBAGENT AUTHORIZATION (user-ratified 2026-07-31): the entry prompt IS the
user's request for every subagent the invoked workflow's ratified form
prescribes — the panel's fresh-context lenses, the close pass, conductor-mode
heavy steps. A harness-level "agents only on user request" default in the
session's system prompt is SATISFIED by that invocation and is never
re-raised as a human gate; only subagent work OUTSIDE a ratified workflow
form needs a fresh ask. Origin: a harness line built into the Claude Code
binary collided with the review workflow's fresh-context mandate at ch13-P1
(`AGENTS.md`, V3 Implementation Plane).

items.title: The model-wave path
items.ezx: Changes to the design model follow one fixed path: edit the sources, rebuild, regenerate the machine-readable ledger, pass the check that the rebuild is byte-identical and the ledger fresh, get human ratification, and re-pin the code mirrors. Semantic changes never go straight into code, and every model-touching act leaves a one-line reflection in the process log.
items.original:
Model-plane changes flow: edit `v3/model/` sources → `tools/v3-model/build.py`
→ regenerated `ledger.md` (`report_ledger.py`) → `tools/v3-model/check.sh`
(byte-identical rebuild plus a fresh-ledger comparison that fails while the
committed ledger is stale — so regeneration precedes the gate; ordering
corrected per 2026-07-28 arm finding #3) → human ratification → drift tests
re-pin the code mirrors; K0-admitted
semantics route here and never as direct code edits, and every
model-touching act appends a one-line K0-gate reflection to the process log.
Source-first is the prescribed flow, not an absolute: the playbook itself
names the escape — "A direct HTML edit requires re-extraction and is the
exception, not the flow" (`v3/design/design-method-playbook.md` §6;
`tools/v3-model/README.md` says the same, provided extraction is rerun so the
sources follow) — so the invariant that actually holds is that sources and
rendered face must end byte-identical, whichever end the edit entered from
(2026-08-18 arm finding #5).

items.title: ADR authoring and lifecycle
items.ezx: Implementation-side decisions are written as numbered architecture decision records with a fixed lifecycle, a mandatory screen against the binding constraints, and a mandatory section saying how to verify the decision still holds. An index lists them all, a watch table tracks declared-but-dormant triggers, and compliance with these records is its own review axis.
items.original:
Implementation-plane decisions become flat-numbered ADRs (`proposed →
accepted → deprecated | superseded`) with mandatory IC-N screen and
Verification, a flat index, a dormant-trigger watch table ("Declared
triggers with no ADR yet — dormant by design, not gaps"), three acceptance
lanes tied to ratification acts, and an ADR compliance review as the third
QA axis.

items.title: Dogfooding runs
items.ezx: Before a chapter closes, the shipped tooling is driven by hand or by script against the real environment — real terminals, real worktrees — to catch the "reality is not what we assumed" failures that test suites structurally miss. Findings go into the process log, and only the user can waive the run, explicitly and on record.
items.original:
Before a chapter close, the shipped operator surface is driven by hand or
script against real substrate (real tmux, worktrees, gate spawns) — "the one
proof tier the CI journeys deliberately exclude", catching "the 'reality
isn't what we assumed' class that test lanes structurally miss"; findings
land as process-log lines; waivable only by the user's explicit recorded
act; from ch9 on includes a real-LLM basic-workflow run.

items.title: Receipt-backed mutation probes
items.ezx: To prove a test can fail, the builder runs a controlled sabotage through a runner: back the file up byte-for-byte, break it, run the tests, restore, and emit a receipt recording the command, exit code, and verified restore. The same spirit applies at writing time: claims about how the environment behaves must carry an actual probe result or a cited source, not an assumption.
items.original:
Builder mutation probes run through `tools/v3-plan/probe_runner.py`:
byte-copy backup ("git-based restore is FORBIDDEN for mutation rollback"),
mutate, run, cmp-verified restore, and a receipt JSON (test command, exit
code, `suite_red`, `restore_verified`, plus a pointer to the full-output
file) that the packet's Build-record probe table cites by id; exit 3 (suite
stayed green) is a build-time finding. Since the ch13-P0 measured hole — all
11 probes ran against an already-red baseline, so every `suite_red` receipt
was vacuous — the runner opens with a GREEN-BASELINE GATE that aborts the run
on a non-green baseline and records the abort as its own class (G20). Its authoring-time sibling:
"Substrate claims are PROBED, not presumed" — any matrix cell resting on
driver/OS behavior carries an in-session probe result or a cited source at
authoring time.

items.title: Pre-registered model-tier experiments
items.ezx: Questions about which AI model tier to use are settled by pre-registered experiments: the design is written once and may not be edited afterwards — only its log and analysis sections may be appended. The first experiment closed with a revert; the second alternates the model tier per chapter, fixed at chapter approval.
items.original:
Model-choice questions run as write-once pre-registered experiments ("only
the §8 log and the §7 analysis entries may be appended; any other edit voids
the pre-registration"): experiment 1 closed REVERT at the ch12 boundary;
experiment 2 alternates the main-thread tier per chapter, fixed at chapter
ratification, with a 5-axis mechanical difficulty index frozen at approve.

items.title: The claim-enumeration audit ritual for authority rewrites
items.ezx: Before rewriting a document that agents execute, every claim the new text will make is first listed as rows, swept, and reviewed by the external model; the change is then written to satisfy exactly those rows. The row file stays behind as the audit record of the change.
items.original:
Before a change rewrites surfaces agents execute, every claim the new text
will make is enumerated as rows, swept, and arm-reviewed; the change is
written to satisfy exactly those rows and the file becomes the post-landing
audit record — used for the Phase-1 authority flip, the autonomy realignment
(AL-1…AL-20), and the ADR-015 migration (with a machine census).

items.title: The per-packet commit triad grammar
items.ezx: Each work item tends to produce the same three commits: the feature commit, an optional aftermath-fix commit, and a process-log commit. The one-item-one-commit rule and the message prefix are written down and machine-checked, but the three-part subject-line pattern itself lives only in practice, in no document.
items.original:
*Practiced, not recorded (in its subject-line half).* From roughly ch7/ch8
onward the commit stream follows a three-part grammar per packet —
`feat(v3): chN-PM — <thing> (packet + code + tests)` → `fix(v3): chN-PM
build-close aftermath — …` (conditional by design: only when aftermath
findings exist) → `docs(v3): process-log — chN-PM …` (verbatim: `e27f33ac` /
`b03ad399` / `76be99d8`; the full triad holds for 22 of the 27 packets from
ch7-P2 on; 185 conventional `(v3)`-scoped commits sit on the post-ADR-015
`v3/` home, 762 across both historical homes). The one-packet-one-commit
rule and the aftermath choreography are written, and the `type(scope)`
prefix is machine-enforced by the commit-msg hook (G17) — but the
subject-line grammar itself appears in no document, including
`docs/commit-message-guidance.md`.
sources: git log (commits e27f33ac / b03ad399 / 76be99d8 — a verbatim triad; 22 of 27 packets from ch7-P2 on)
flags: practiced, not recorded (in its subject-line half)

items.title: The human-gate presentation discipline
items.ezx: Whenever a decision reaches the human, the message follows eight fixed rules: one decision per message, all context included, a clear statement of what the human judges versus what machines already verified, the risk and its reversibility, and always a recommendation with reasoning. A question whose answer needs more than one word is treated as a defect in the presentation, not in the human.
items.original:
Whenever a decision reaches the human — a STOP, a flag-bearing approve, a
ratification, a boundary verdict, a close act — the presentation follows
eight adopted rules: one decision per message; self-contained context ("the
reader assumed to hold NONE of the process state in their head"); the ROLE
statement (what the human judges vs. what machines already verified); the
RISK statement with reversibility; a RECOMMENDATION with reasoning, always
("the human adjudicates a proposal, never composes from a blank page"); a
closed decision vocabulary; a roadmap-then-steps cadence; and "a ONE-WORD
answer must suffice — a question whose answer needs an essay is a
presentation defect".

items.title: `check_docs.py`, the composite doc-gate runner
items.ezx: A recurring wrapper procedure that runs the canonical document gates in per-mode bundles — quick, packet-approve, chapter-close — and prints what it does not cover. It is deliberately never a gate itself: the gates it calls remain the real authority.
items.original:
A composite RUNNER for the doc-family gates: recurring `quick` /
`packet-approve` / `chapter-close` bundles select and run the canonical gate
commands, handle timeouts, go red if any member gate is red, and print what
they do NOT cover. The repo denies it gate status by declaration ("WRAPPER,
never a replacement … never a gate-point substitute") and the ledger keeps
that denial; as a recurring procedure through which work flows it is a
Mechanism. Reclassified from Unclassified (U1) per the 2026-07-28 arm round
(finding #10).
sources: v3/implementation/README.md §5.5 ("composite RUNNER for the doc-family gates")

items.title: Finding triage and disposition routing
items.ezx: Every finding raised by anyone — a reviewer lens, the outside model, the human — must be given a written disposition: folded in, narrowed, declined, pushed to build, or handed to a named owner such as the chapter boundary or a later chapter. Each one carries a severity from a shared scale and a one-line reason, and every round reports the tally.
items.original:
Every finding from any round — panel lens, external arm, or the user — gets
an explicit recorded disposition: `folded` / `narrowed` / `declined` /
`deferred-to-build`, or an ownership ROUTE (`boundary-review`,
`later-chapter`, `declined`, `approve-ratified`) that names where the
question goes next. Each carries a severity graded on the v1-inherited
ontology `docs/reviewer-severity-ontology.md` and a one-line why, and the
round report carries the disposition tally. This is what makes fix-by-default
(P10) affordable: the default routes effort, never truth, and a declined
finding leaves a record of the ground it was declined on — the routine
`declined: out of threat model` line is P15 in operation.
sources: docs/reviewer-severity-ontology.md (the P0–P3 scale, inherited from the v1 plane)

items.title: The aftermath fold loop
items.ezx: Findings that arrive after a work item is already closed are not lost and not silently patched: they fold back into the same work order and its build record through the same reconciliation pass a normal review fold takes, and land as one fix commit carrying document, code, and tests together.
items.original:
Post-close findings fold into the packet's claim surface and the Build
record's Aftermath section through the SAME lens-4 reconciliation pass as a
panel fold — "an aftermath fold IS a fold". The aftermath `fix(v3)` commit
carries packet + code + tests together and may extend the `mutation_boundary`
aftermath-scoped, audited at its own sha; process-log lines ride separate
docs commits. The loop closes the gap that would otherwise open between "the
packet is committed" and "the packet is true".
sources: v3/implementation/README.md §4 ("an aftermath fold IS a fold")

items.title: The re-derivation arm procedure (the ch13 pattern)
items.ezx: When a line of work hits a measured quality floor it is not patched in place: it is superseded forward onto a fresh branch and derived again phase by phase, with four named roles — the human as ratifier and relay, an orchestrating session, an executing session, and a verifying outside arm — each phase handed over as a paste-ready, self-contained instruction block and closed by a filed verdict.
items.original:
*One executed instance; the role choreography is homed only in its own plan.*
When a ratified line hits a measured semantic drift floor, it is superseded
FORWARD onto an oracle branch ("Supersede FORWARD — no history surgery") and
re-derived phase by phase, run by four roles — user (ratifier/relay), general
(orchestrator, fresh session), executor (fresh session), arm (fresh-context
verifier) — with paste-ready self-contained instruction blocks and per-phase
verdicts filed in an `-arm/` directory. Scope note, folded from the
2026-08-18 arm round (finding #6): this four-role relay is NOT the general
staffing model for heavy v3 work — that is M7's conductor architecture,
homed in `v3/implementation/README.md` §4. The re-derivation plan scopes
itself explicitly to its own hand-over ("the executing sessions read THIS
document"), and the record shows no later chapter running the relay.
flags: one executed instance; the role choreography is homed only in its own plan

items.title: Skill-ification: template first, skill only after live validation
items.ezx: A new way of working starts as a document plus a checklist that a human or agent follows by hand. Only after enough live runs prove the shape does it become a packaged skill — and even then the canonical documents keep authority: if the skill and the documents disagree, the documents win and the disagreement is logged as friction.
items.original:
A process flow starts as a template + checklist executed manually; only after
repeated live use validates the shape does it become a repo-local skill, with
content authority staying in the canonical files — "If this skill and those
files disagree, the files win — and the disagreement becomes a friction-log
line". Executed once, at the ch6→ch7 boundary (2026-07-08): the written
criterion was "2–3 real tasks validate the shape" and it was met "several
times over — 14 live packets across chapters 4–6, the last 10 on a
structurally unchanged template". The authority boundary is stated in the
same section: the template, the projection checklist, the `REV-*` registry
and the contract-draft template stay canonical in `v3/implementation/`, while
the skill carries procedure plus the distilled failure-class registry and is
amended at chapter boundaries only. The rule is P9's empiricism applied to
tooling — the skill is a mechanics relocation, never an authority move — and
the repo-local scope is deliberate: the skill is NOT promoted to the global
skill set, "the corpus pattern has a sample size of one, so nothing is
generalized yet".
sources: .claude/skills/CreateTaskPacket/SKILL.md ("If this skill and those files disagree, the files win")

items.title: The task packet
items.ezx: The packet is the self-contained work order a build runs from: it carries the plan step, the exact slice of the design ledger it implements, the full text of everything the builder needs, machine-checkable gates, a row-by-row record of where each requirement came from, and the acceptance tests. Its shape is enforced by writing disciplines more than by a fill-in skeleton.
items.original:
The executable working unit of the build loop: header (plan step, autonomy
stage, predicted `projection|invention` class), declared `ledger_slice`,
materialized `## Sizing/risk` record, full-text operative material,
in-context notes, embedding gates + `mutation_boundary` machine block, the
`packet_rows` provenance manifest (`anchored`/`derived`/`new-decision`),
pre-approval flags with routes, acceptance (CT-*/CHK-*/REV-* + discipline
and family inventories), Build record, and one `packet_metrics` machine
block written at build close; since the ch14-p2a boundary a packet may
additionally declare the opt-in `instrument_manifest` block that confines the
instrument-landing commit exception (M2). Live packets additionally carry a semantic
spine hardened by write-time disciplines rather than template slots: a wide
`## Claim`, its enumerated dimensions, canonical contract matrices with
collapsed-lane member inventories, and a Mirrored Surface Map naming every
restatement of a canonical row (shape by discipline, not by skeleton).

items.title: The chapter contract-draft
items.ezx: One chapter's design decisions written as numbered normative rows in a single file, with a status field (draft, ratified, reopened, realized) and an append-only ratification history. The bar for a row: it must stay true and decidable even if all the code were deleted and rebuilt from the work orders.
items.original:
One chapter's memo-born surface as normative `C<n>` rows: JSON meta block
(`status: draft|ratified|reopened|realized`), non-normative Context, the
contract-rows table, append-only ratification history (`{date, arms,
commit}`), and the close-time `realized_map`. Content law: the bar for a row
is tree-independence ("if `v3/src` were deleted and rewritten from the
packets, would this row still be true and decidable?"), every normative
statement is a C-row — an iff-clause discovered in prose is a review
finding, never a legal edit path — and the round-0 skeleton answers the
Control-Model checklist in the non-normative Context.
sources: v3/implementation/contract-draft-template.md ("the canonical FORM authority … on any mismatch the TEMPLATE wins and the lint is the bug")
v3/implementation/contracts/ (7 instances: ch8, ch9, ch11, ch12, ch13, ch13-v2, ch14)

items.title: The model ledger
items.ezx: The generated, do-not-edit machine face of the design model: four registries covering deferred items, invariant rules, rejected names, and domains. It is the contract surface between model and code that every work order anchors to.
items.original:
The generated machine face of the model — "GENERATED — do not edit" — four
registries: the 140-item deferral ledger, the 116-rule invariant catalog,
the 54-name rejection registry, and the domain registry; it is "the
model↔code contract surface every packet anchors to".

items.title: The core-model source corpus
items.ezx: The hand-authored sources of the design model: annotated section files, protocol pseudocode stored as deltas rather than copies, full config snapshots, and one-record-per-fact JSON files — all rebuilt byte-identically into a single model document.
items.original:
The model's authoring surface: `sections/NN-<id>.html` with
`[[@code/@fold/@absent/@invariants]]` markers, protocol pseudocode in
unit-delta form (`units/<block>/<unit>.txt` + `deltas/<block>.json` — "a new
level is a delta, not a copy"), full config snapshots, one-record-per-fact
`records/absent|invariants/*.json`, and `manifest.json` — rebuilt
byte-identically into `core-model.html`.

items.title: The plan chapter
items.ezx: The chapter as a planning unit: a header with the ratification date and autonomy stage, scope and boundaries, a table of work items with predicted class and execution mode, deliverables, and a definition of done. Its shape is a convention described in prose — there is no written template.
items.original:
*Shape by convention, no written template.* The ordering/scoping unit:
chapter header with ratified date and autonomy stage, scope and boundaries,
a `Packets and flow mode` table with per-packet predicted class and mode,
deliverables and DoD; chapter 1 additionally holds the IC/PI intake tables
and the §1.4 coverage inventory. The packet table is the LATER form, not a
universal one: at this head the first `Packets and flow mode` section is
§6.7, and the earlier calibration chapters do not each carry one — §3.7 says
chapter 3 runs with "no task packets: the ledger slices here are thin"
(2026-08-18 arm finding #4). What the process authority requires of every
later chapter is the scope/deliverables/acceptance triple
(`v3/implementation/README.md` §3); the packet table joined as the
packet-derivation surface once packets became the working unit. New chapters
append through the §1.3 map-extension mechanism with an explicit build-order
slot — the mechanism ch11–ch14 all entered through.
flags: shape by convention, no written template

items.title: The ADR
items.ezx: A numbered architecture decision record with a status lifecycle line, context, the decision, alternatives considered, a mandatory screen against the binding constraints, and a mandatory verification section. The index file adds a summary table and a watch table for declared-but-dormant triggers.
items.original:
`ADR-NNN` with Status lifecycle line, Links, Context, Decision, Alternatives
Considered, a mandatory IC-N Screen, Consequences, mandatory Verification,
and Related; the index README adds the flat id/title/status/date table and
the dormant-trigger watch table.

items.title: The process-log entry
items.ezx: One dated, append-only line per observation in a single long log file, with the outcome appended to the same line later, at boundary-review time. In practice recent entries have grown into multi-paragraph dated narratives while the log's own header still prescribes one line — the written form rule was never amended.
items.original:
*Form drift: practiced form has outgrown the recorded form.* Append-only
one-liner: "`- YYYY-MM-DD · <phase/chapter> · <observation>`", with "`→
<outcome>`" appended at boundary-review time. The file has grown from ~4,800
lines at the 2026-07-28 fold to 6,157 at this one, and the recent entries are
multi-paragraph dated narratives (boundary-review records run dozens of lines
with bolded verdict headings) — the declared one-line form was never amended
to match, so the divergence is a project fact about the log, not a violation
anyone is policing.
flags: form drift: practiced form has outgrown the recorded form

items.title: The learned-rule registry row
items.ezx: A distilled lesson-learned as one table row: a rule ID, an imperative rule sentence, and provenance pointing at the document section it changed and the dated log line it was born from. Rules are admitted by a written procedure, and a sibling registry holds the standing review rules.
items.original:
Distilled failure-class rules as table rows: `R-<SLUG>` + imperative rule
statement + provenance citing the README/template section and the dated log
line, with a written admission procedure; sibling form: the `REV-*` standing
review rules in `v3/implementation/task-packet-template.md` §3. The registry
is 16 rows at this head, DOWN from 23 at the 2026-07-28 fold: rows are
absorbed into broader ones rather than accumulated (R-NUMERIC-LADDER into
R-DIMENSIONS, R-FIELD-LISTS into R-DELEGATION-CLOSURE, both at the ch13
boundary), and a surviving row grows scope extensions in place, each dated by
the boundary that adopted it. The form is therefore a shrinking-and-deepening
registry, not a changelog.

items.title: The panel report block
items.ezx: The verdict document of every review round: exactly which bytes were reviewed, the machine-gate results, the five lens reports, the findings with their dispositions, and the verdict. A verdict given in chat without this block is itself a process defect; the block is handed back in-thread rather than stored, and its residue lands in the packet and the log.
items.original:
The verdict artifact of every review round: packet basis (sha256 @ commit,
worktree state), tier-0 results, re-run mode with transcript-verified model
ids, Gate Coverage Matrix, five lens reports, findings + disposition tally,
yield curve + plateau counter, size + growth, and the verdict — "a verdict
delivered in commentary without the report block is a workflow defect".
Ephemeral: handed back in-thread; residue lands in packet flags/Build record
and the log.

items.title: The chapter-trace / journey golden test
items.ezx: A model walkthrough turned into an executable test: a declarative fixture listing the steps, the expected event transcript, and post-condition checks. The convention when lifting a test to a new level is that an assertion may never be weakened.
items.original:
The model trace as an executable expectation: a declarative fixture (step
list + final `[seq, opId]` transcript expectation + post-condition checkers)
typed in `v3/src/testkit/traceHarness.ts`, with the level-lifting convention
that "may never weaken a trace assertion". Instances: `v3/src/l0aTrace.test.ts`
… `l2aTrace.test.ts`, `l0dJourney.test.ts`. The file-level shape is
convention; the fixture data shape is specified.

items.title: The invariant-disposition map
items.ezx: A single machine-validated file that assigns every one of the 116 model invariants to one enforcement class — test, type/schema, checker, or review. No work order may declare an assignment that contradicts a row here.
items.original:
A one-instance, machine-validated classification: a rubric for four
enforcement classes (`test` / `type/schema` / `checker` / `review`) plus one
machine block mapping all 116 ledger invariants; "no packet may declare a
disposition that contradicts a row here (the packet↔map lock)".

items.title: The arm-pin table
items.ezx: An append-only table recording which external reviewer model is pinned, at what reasoning effort, and — since August 2026 — over which transport, changeable only at chapter boundaries. Consumers read the last row, and a review whose output header disagrees with the pin is an invalid verdict. Each arm run additionally files its own bundle of prompts, raw transcripts, and verdicts in the repository.
items.original:
Append-only `Pinned at | Model | Reasoning effort | Transport | Note` rows —
the transport column added at the ch13 boundary (2026-08-14) per the
2026-08-10 user ruling — revisable at chapter boundaries only; consumers read
the last row, and an invocation whose output header disagrees with the pin is
an invalid verdict. The file carries operational notes beside the table
(transport rules, the serial-regression-run hazard, the tier-record rule), so
it is the pin's home and the transport's home at once. *Bundle half, thinly
recorded:* arm runs file per-phase bundles — charter, round prompts, raw
`-out.txt` transcripts, verdicts, review records — in `-arm/` directories;
the convention is executed consistently but authorized by a single sentence
in `v3/implementation/ch13-rederivation-plan.md`.
flags: the bundle-filing convention is executed consistently but authorized by a single sentence

items.title: The pre-registered experiment report
items.ezx: The report form of a pre-registered experiment: a status line carrying the write-once rule, an analysis-and-verdict section, and an append-only log. The middle sections vary between the two existing instances, and there is no written template.
items.original:
*Shape by convention across two instances, no written template.* The stable
skeleton is thin: a Status line carrying the write-once rule, a §7
analysis/verdict block, and a §8 append-only log; the middle sections
(hypothesis / design / metrics / stop rules) vary between the two instances.
flags: shape by convention across two instances, no written template

items.title: The design memo and external-study forms
items.ezx: The design-side working papers the process consumes: topic memos whose filenames carry an open/closed lifecycle prefix and a routing index, and studies of outside systems mapped onto the model's levels with precise file-and-line citations and learn/avoid/orthogonal verdicts.
items.original:
Model-plane working documents the v3 process consumes: topic memos with
`_open-`/`_closed-` lifecycle naming and a routing README, and
external-system studies mapping one system onto v3 levels with `file:line`
citations and LEARN/AVOID/ORTHOGONAL verdicts.

items.title: The implementation contract (IC-*/PI-* rows)
items.ezx: The register of binding implementation constraints: IC rows that each must map to a test, a check, or a decision record, plus a plan-intake checklist realized as tables whose status flips when a chapter completes.
items.original:
The binding constraint register the plan consumes: `IC-*` rows, each of
which "maps to one or more of: an acceptance/contract test, a
schema/lint/CI check, or an ADR", and the `PI-*` plan-intake checklist —
realized as the chapter-1 intake tables whose status flips at chapter DoD.

items.title: The deferred-hardening register (FH-* rows)
items.ezx: A durable list of robustness gaps knowingly postponed at a human decision point. Each row records where the gap came from, the premise under which deferring was accepted, a proposed (not yet ratified) landing spot, and the trigger for revisiting it — so the deferral is never silently lost.
items.original:
Implementation-plane robustness gaps consciously deferred at a human
decision point — each row carries provenance, the ratified premise, a
proposed (not yet ratified) landing, and a revisit trigger: "a durable
record so the deferral is never silently lost"; the terminal home for
accept-now resolutions of `4:flagged-approve` STOPs (FH-1 was born from the
ch12-P2 approve).

items.title: The drift unit map
items.ezx: A machine-readable manifest that pairs every unit of the design model with its realization status and the exact code reference that realizes it. Two independent gates read it: the drift tests assert its key set equals the model's source tree and that every code reference resolves, and the coverage checker uses it as one leg of a three-way lock.
items.original:
`v3/src/drift/unitMap.json`: the machine manifest mapping every ledger unit to
its realization status and code reference. It is the only artifact-form both
verification families read — the drift suite (G5) asserts its key set equals
the `v3/model/units/` tree and that every `codeRef` resolves under
`tsc --noEmit`, and the coverage accounting (G4) locks it against the ledger
and the packets as the third leg of the three-way lock. Listed as its own
form rather than as part of the model ledger because its authority is
code-side: it is written and maintained on the implementation plane, while
the ledger it is checked against is generated on the model plane.
sources: tools/v3-plan/check_coverage.py (the third leg of the lock)

items.title: Pre-push hook → `pnpm ci:local`
items.ezx: Every git push runs the full local CI battery, whose v3 part chains the six v3 quality checks — lint, typecheck, tests, decision-record check, coverage lock, and packet lint. Any red result blocks the push.
items.original:
*Machine-enforced.* Every `git push` runs the full local CI gate
(`.githooks/pre-push`, `core.hooksPath=.githooks`), whose v3 quality child
is `pnpm v3:lint && v3:typecheck && v3:test && v3:adr-check && v3:coverage
&& v3:packet-lint` (`scripts/ci-local.sh` line 327); any red blocks the
push. The same script rebuilds `PATH` to HIDE the external arm binary for the run,
so the external arm can never execute inside the machine chokepoint — the two
verification families stay decorrelated by construction (P10). The hiding has
a declared opt-out: one documented environment flag restores the original
PATH, and the run then announces "local PATH preserved" (`scripts/ci-local.sh`
lines 33–35; 2026-08-18 arm finding #8 — the ledger states the opt-out rather
than an absolute).

items.title: GitHub Actions "V3 checks"
items.ezx: The same six v3 quality checks run in GitHub Actions on every push to the main branch — the only piece of the shared v1 CI that touches the v3 work.
items.original:
*Machine-enforced.* The same six v3 bridges run on every push to `main`
(`.github/workflows/release.yml` lines 74–75) — the only v1 CI surface that
touches v3.

items.title: Packet/draft lint (`check_packet.py`)
items.ezx: A linter validates work orders and contract drafts: machine-block schemas, contract references that must resolve to a ratified draft, complete lane IDs, and that ratified rows are byte-equal to what git history says was ratified. Its stricter modes gate approvals, chapter closes, and the after-build audit.
items.original:
*Machine-enforced (plain mode in G1/G2); its strict modes are
procedure-triggered.* Validates the packet and draft claim families:
machine-block schemas, `contract:chN-<surface>#Cn` refs resolving to a
"ratified-or-later draft; reopened does NOT qualify", lane-id completeness,
ratification-block shape with `git show` C-row equality. `--forbid-reopened`
gates packet approve / chapter close / process flips; `--post-build <sha>`
is the build-close audit ("no CI surface runs this mode").
sources: v3/implementation/README.md §4 ("no CI surface runs this mode")

items.title: The coverage three-way lock (`check_coverage.py`)
items.ezx: A script asserts that the coverage arithmetic closes: the declared work slices together cover the model inventory with no orphans and no undeclared double owners, the unit map matches the source tree, and at build close what a packet owns equals what was actually realized.
items.original:
*Machine-enforced (default mode in G1/G2); `--fold-time`
procedure-triggered at approve.* Asserts the union of declared
`ledger_slice`s covers the model inventory, no orphans, no undeclared double
owners, `unitMap.json` keyset == the units tree, and (build-close default)
owned == realized with matching dispositions. THREE modes with distinct gate
points: default = build-close, `--fold-time` = the approve-time gate,
`--assert-closed` = the closure check that answers "is the plan concrete
enough". The invariant lane REQUIRES `v3/implementation/invariant-disposition-map.md`
(A11) from packet ch5-P2 on — the map's key set must equal ledger §2, a
packet-declared invariant must carry the SAME disposition as the map, and
realized rows must have packet owners; `--disposition-map` overrides the path
as the negative-test seam. Its declared inputs are the model tree, the
generated ledger, the packet files, `unitMap.json` and the disposition map —
it does not read the plan (the false `G4 consumes A5` edge was dropped at this
fold, 2026-08-18 arm finding #10).
sources: tools/v3-plan/check_coverage.py ("This is the BUILD-CLOSE gate point"; --fold-time: "the APPROVE-TIME gate point")

items.title: The drift-test trio + source hygiene
items.ezx: Drift tests re-read the generated model ledger at test time and fail if the code's mirrored lists differ from it; a sibling locks a key map to the model's source tree, and another bans raw control bytes in sources. They run inside the normal v3 test suite.
items.original:
*Machine-enforced.* `v3/src/drift/rejectionNames.test.ts` and
`domainRegistry.test.ts` re-parse `v3/model/ledger.md` at test time and
require set equality with the code mirrors, while `unitMap.test.ts` locks
`unitMap.json`'s key set to the `v3/model/units/` source tree with
resolvable codeRefs (PI-3, ADR-007); `sourceHygiene.test.ts` bans raw
control bytes. Runs in `pnpm v3:test` → G1/G2.

items.title: ESLint architecture fences + strict tsconfig
items.ezx: Per-directory lint rules turn architecture decisions into hard lint errors — banned imports, no direct wall-clock reads, module boundaries, the CLI write boundary — alongside strict type checking. The v3 config is the sole lint authority for the v3 tree.
items.original:
*Machine-enforced.* Per-directory import/syntax bans carrying ADR decisions
into lint errors — "CHK-D-NOCLOCK: no direct wall-clock read — time flows
through the injected TimeSource", module import boundaries, the CLI write
boundary — in `v3/eslint.config.mjs` (root config ignores `v3/**`, making it
the sole lint authority), plus `pnpm v3:typecheck` under strict options.

items.title: ADR integrity check
items.ezx: A script checks the decision records' integrity: valid statuses, no dangling references between records, supersede links pointing both ways, no cycles, and an index consistent with the files.
items.original:
*Machine-enforced.* `v3/adr/check.sh` (`pnpm v3:adr-check`): status enum
validity, no dangling `ADR-NNN` refs, supersede reciprocity in both
directions, no cycles, index-row consistency.

items.title: Model freshness check
items.ezx: A script verifies that the model sources rebuild the published model document and the generated ledger byte-identically. The method requires it to pass before any model commit, but no hook or CI lane runs it automatically — a person or procedure has to invoke it.
items.original:
*Machine script, procedure-triggered.* `tools/v3-model/check.sh` requires
`v3/model/` sources to rebuild `core-model.html` byte-identically and
`ledger.md` to be regenerable byte-identically ("check: FAIL — ledger.md is
stale"); mandated by the playbook's "edit sources → build.py → check.sh must
pass before commit" — no hook or CI invokes it.
sources: v3/design/design-method-playbook.md §6 ("edit sources → build.py → check.sh must pass before commit")

items.title: The contract-draft ratification act
items.ezx: No work order may anchor to a contract draft the human has not ratified on named bytes, and re-ratifying after a reopen is just as permanently human. The linter checks the paperwork's shape, but performing the act itself deliberately sits outside every machine surface.
items.original:
*Procedure-enforced (machine half in G3).* No packet may anchor to a draft
the human has not ratified on named bytes; re-ratification after a reopen is
"permanently human, exactly like ratification"; the lint verifies block
shape and C-row equality; performing the act itself sits outside every
machine surface.

items.title: The STOP registry, verdict-action matrix, and standing human checkpoints
items.ezx: The loop halts and asks the human in four named situations, each with a canonical token — late signals or divergence, plan-boundary conflicts, a round watchdog or plateau, and approvals that carry flags. Flag-bearing approvals always go to the human; flag-free ones became autonomous from chapter 8; chapter ratification, the divergence stop, and draft ratification are never automated.
items.original:
*Procedure-enforced.* The loop halts to the human on four STOP classes with
canonical minted tokens (`1:late-b-signal`/`1:divergence`/`1:open-choice`,
`2:*` plan-boundary conflicts, `3:watchdog` at 8 rounds / `3:plateau`,
`4:flagged-approve`); flag-bearing approves are human at every trust stage,
flag-free approves autonomous from ch8; chapter ratification, the divergence
stop, and draft ratification are never automated. Token values are
lint-validated post hoc in `packet_metrics.stops[].type` (G3). The registry's
partner surface is the VERDICT-ACTION MATRIX, which decides at every loop
event whether the machine proceeds or the human is required — the two
together are the autonomy envelope's control, and the entry-mode trust dial
(M7) is their session-entry face. One further standing checkpoint sits beside
the four classes: the FIRST packet of a new task class is human-approved
"regardless of trust stage", so a new kind of work never enters through the
autonomous door (2026-08-18 arm finding #2).

items.title: The two mandatory external-arm gates
items.ezx: On the autonomous path a second, different AI model must sign off twice: once before the build starts, on the exact final content, and once at build close, including a pass that verifies every declared test can actually fail. If that external model is unavailable, work stops — it is never silently skipped, and only the human can waive a gate.
items.original:
*Procedure-enforced, with machine-guarded invocation (M5).* On the
autonomous path: (1) APPROVE gate — build starts only on an arm verdict
citing the final hash with zero fold-now findings; (2) BUILD-CLOSE gate —
the packet is done only on a clean sha-citing verdict including the
mandatory sensitivity pass verifying every declared inventory member "DRIVEN
and ABLE TO FAIL in the built test bodies". An unavailable arm is a
verified-preflight-failure BLOCKER → STOP, "never a silent skip"; a waive is
the human's explicit act per gate.

items.title: The chapter Definition of Done
items.ezx: A chapter only counts as done when the whole checklist holds, regardless of the state of the code: tests green, intake tables flipped, born decision records accepted, the log review held, the full local CI green including the root suite, the hands-on dogfooding checkpoint, and every referenced contract draft closed out.
items.original:
*Procedure-enforced, composing machine gates.* "A chapter without these is
not done regardless of code state": contract + drift tests green, intake
tables flipped, born ADRs accepted, the process-log review held, full `pnpm
ci:local` green (root suite included), the dogfooding checkpoint
(user-waivable only, recorded), and the three draft-close conditions — zero
reopened drafts, every referenced draft `realized` or `superseded`, the
draft-metrics close line. Supersession alone does not discharge the
obligation: "a superseded draft's realization obligation TRANSFERS to its
successor surface, which must itself stand `realized` at the close"
(`v3/implementation/README.md` §6) — without that clause the DoD would be
materially weaker, since a chapter could close by superseding its way out
(2026-08-18 arm finding #7).

items.title: The chapter-close scanners
items.ezx: Two scanner scripts run at chapter close: one goes red while any deferred-work marker addressed to the closing chapter remains — a malformed marker also fails — and the other errors when a contract-row lane is missing from the realized map. They are machine scripts, but a procedure has to run them; the normal CI does not.
items.original:
*Machine scripts, procedure-triggered (absent from G1/G2).*
`tools/v3-plan/check_deferred.py` (`pnpm v3:deferred --closed chN`): a close
goes red while any canonical `DEFERRED(chN[-pM]):` marker addressed to the
chapter remains, and a malformed marker is fail-closed red.
`tools/v3-plan/check_realized_map.py` (`pnpm v3:realized-map`): a
manifest-reffed C-row lane missing from the realized map is a hard error
("omissions are the defect class"); the map additionally gets a detached,
non-blocking external-arm audit settled before the next chapter's close.

items.title: The mechanical pre-commit gate (`commit_helper.py`)
items.ezx: An opt-in commit wrapper refuses staged files outside the declared scope and any staged file that still has unstaged edits, and always runs the composite document gate. The judgment half of the checklist stays explicitly with the caller.
items.original:
*Machine-enforced when used (opt-in wrapper, no hook).* `pnpm v3:commit`
refuses staged files outside the declared scope and any staged file carrying
unstaged edits (COMMIT-03), and always runs the doc-gate composite; the
judgment half of the checklist stays explicitly CALLER-ANSWERED.

items.title: The write-time sizing/risk hard stops
items.ezx: At work-order writing time, six inherited risk axes plus sizing triggers define combinations where splitting the work is required, not advised. The outcome is recorded in the work order itself, and this is the only hard sizing rail — the review-round size thresholds are merely advisory.
items.original:
*Procedure-enforced.* Template §2 step 0: the six v1-inherited risk axes
plus v3 sizing triggers with hard-stop combinations that are
"split-REQUIRED — split is not advisory", materialized as the packet's
`## Sizing/risk` record; the only hard sizing rail (the round-report size
thresholds are advisory).

items.title: The verification-surface tooling review
items.ezx: Any tool that becomes part of the checking machinery — a gate, a wrapper over gates, a choreography runner, reviewer infrastructure — gets a review by the external AI model before its first load-bearing use. If it is disputed whether a tool falls in this class, the default is that it does.
items.original:
*Procedure-enforced.* Any tool participating in the verification surface — a
tier-0 gate, a wrapper over ratified gates, a choreography executor, arm
infrastructure — receives an external-arm review before its first
load-bearing use; a disputed classification "defaults to the arm
(fail-closed)".

items.title: The commit-message policy hook
items.ezx: A commit-message hook rejects any commit whose subject does not match the conventional type(scope): grammar. It is v1 machinery that the v3 commit stream also runs through, and the machine-enforced half of the commit-triad practice.
items.original:
*Machine-enforced.* `.githooks/commit-msg` runs the commit-policy validator
on every commit under the same `core.hooksPath` that carries G1; a subject
not matching the conventional `type(scope):` grammar is rejected
(`src/v11/shared/commitPolicy/commitMessagePolicy.ts`) — v1 machinery the v3
commit stream runs through, and the machine-enforced half of M14's grammar.

items.title: The tier-0 selftest armor
items.ezx: The four Python checker gates first prove themselves against throwaway fixtures before running: each failure dimension must actually go red, plus one green control showing the reds are not ambient. The ADR gate's bridge carries no such self-test. A decayed selftest turns the main CI gates red.
items.original:
*Machine-enforced.* The four Python checker bridges chain `--selftest &&
<run>` (`package.json`: `v3:coverage`, `v3:packet-lint`, `v3:deferred`,
`v3:realized-map`) — the ADR bridge (`v3:adr-check`, plain bash) carries no
selftest (2026-07-28 arm finding #6): throwaway fixtures prove "each cross-check dimension
actually fails red, plus one green control proving the failures are not
ambient" — the standing mechanized floor the arm review (G16) sits on top of
("selftest armor scales with the declared surface"); a decayed selftest reds
G1/G2.
sources: v3/implementation/README.md §5.5 ("selftest armor scales with the declared surface")

items.title: The model↔code divergence stop
items.ezx: If implementation work uncovers a bug or a gap in the design model, the loop must stop. The fix is never made quietly in the code: it goes back through the design side and returns as a regenerated machine ledger. This is a gate a human must honour — no script can detect that a discovery is model-shaped.
items.original:
*Procedure-enforced.* A model bug or gap surfacing during implementation is a
mandatory stop: "NEVER silently patched in code" — it routes through the
model plane (M8) and returns via the regenerated ledger, user-gated on the
way. Listed as its own gate rather than only as P1's content because it is
the one control that can halt a running build for a reason no machine surface
can see: the machine gates below it police form, while this one polices where
a discovery is allowed to be fixed. Its downstream half IS machine-enforced —
once the model moves, G5's drift trio and G8's freshness check make the code
side follow or go red.

items.title: The probe-runner green-baseline gate
items.ezx: Before a deliberate sabotage test runs, the tool first proves the test suite was green to begin with. If the baseline is already red, the run is aborted and recorded as such, because a "the suite went red" receipt from an already-red suite proves nothing.
items.original:
*Machine-enforced.* `tools/v3-plan/probe_runner.py` opens every probe with a
baseline run: a non-green baseline ABORTS the probe, is recorded as its own
receipt class ("baseline": "RED — instrument broken, receipt would be
vacuous"), and exits nonzero; a green baseline is recorded in the receipt.
Born from a measured hole rather than a worry — at ch13-P0 all 11 probes ran
against an already-red baseline, so every `suite_red` receipt was vacuous.
The runner additionally byte-verifies restoration and treats a suite that
stays green under mutation as a blind probe with its own exit code. It is the
instrument that makes M11's receipts admissible, and the clearest instance of
P7 turned on the verification tooling itself.
sources: tools/v3-plan/probe_runner.py (the GREEN-BASELINE GATE docstring; the ch13-P0 measured hole)

items.title: The Stryker mutation-testing pilot
items.ezx: A mutation-testing pilot that is wired up but deliberately blocks nothing: it mutates exactly one file and appears in no hook, CI lane, or done-checklist. It runs beside the external review for two chapters until a chapter-boundary evaluation decides whether to adopt it.
items.original:
Wired but deliberately non-gating: it mutates exactly one file
(`src/emit/opId.ts`) and appears in no hook, CI lane, or DoD. It ran as a
dual-run beside arm gate-2 for two chapters, and the ch13 boundary review
(2026-08-14) CLOSED it on its own data: **STOP** — in this setup, over nine runs, it surfaced no defect the arm had
not already found, against a cost of ~12m48s per run plus a maintenance
surface and structural subprocess blindness. The
wiring stays; the usage lessons are recorded (whole-file scope rather than
delta; detector role rather than trend role; the sandbox-path abort is a
configuration issue in this setup), and a revival would be "incremental + delta +
boundary-trend, never a per-packet gate" (`v3/implementation/process-log.md`
line 5790). It stays Unclassified for the same reason as before and one new
one: it can stop nothing (not a Check/Gate), no work flows through it (not a
Mechanism), and it is now a CLOSED experiment whose apparatus is deliberately
left in place — the taxonomy has no slot for a retired-but-wired instrument.

The stop is also the cleanest worked example of the process judging its own
additions: the pilot was pre-registered with a dual-run window, ran to the
window's end, and was disposed against its recorded yield rather than against
anyone's prior on mutation testing.

items.title: The autonomy trajectory (calibration → measurement → chaining)
items.ezx: A declared, dated position on how far the loop is currently trusted to run alone: the calibration stage closed with a pilot chapter, the current measurement stage runs unattended work with after-the-fact audits, and a future chaining stage would deliver whole chapters through the older product-side machinery.
items.original:
A staged ramp with named stages: CALIBRATION closed with the ch7 pilot;
MEASUREMENT (ch8 onward) runs autonomous flag-free packets with post-hoc
boundary audits of the `detector_misses` stream; CHAINING is the declared
future — chapter-level delivery through the v1 `ExecutePairflowPlan` and
pairflow doc-bubbles, with "when the accounting closes" as its stated
concreteness criterion. It resists the taxonomy because it is none of the
four types: not a timeless rule, not a procedure work flows through, not a
document shape, not a control that can stop anything. It is a dated STATE —
the process's self-description of where on the autonomy dial it currently
stands, and the thing every autonomy element (P3, G10, M7) is calibrated
against. Listing it keeps that calibration point visible
instead of implicit.

items.title: The ch11 model-sync carve-out
items.ezx: A ratified one-off exception that allowed named gates to stay red at exactly one approval, with anything beyond the named list blocking. Its window has since expired, and it stays listed as the standing precedent for how a mandatory gate may lawfully be red.
items.original:
A ratified, one-packet-scoped amendment to gate preconditions — three named
drift lanes and nine enumerated coverage items were allowed red at exactly
one approve, "any deviation beyond BLOCKS" — whose window is now SPENT: it
expired at ch11-P0 build-close (ch11's contract is `realized`, and two later
chapters have closed since), leaving the drift trio and the fold-time gate
unconditionally binding again. It stays listed as the standing precedent for
how a mandatory gate may lawfully be red — an instance, not a form; a dated,
self-expiring exception the taxonomy has no slot for.

coreThree.title: The two planes must not shear
coreThree.ezx: Every other surface takes its meaning from the design model being the single semantic truth: the ledger is its machine face, packets project it, drift tests lock it. Without this principle the remaining machinery verifies nothing in particular.

coreThree.title: Autonomy is proportional to contract density; the loop stops exactly where a new semantic decision is needed
coreThree.ezx: This is the constitution of who decides: the stop registry, the ratification acts, the trust dial, and the flagged-versus-flag-free split are all its projections. Losing it collapses the process into all-human ceremony or unaccountable autonomy. The 2026-08-18 run defended the STOP registry itself in this slot rather than the principle; both are kept, because the registry plus the verdict-action matrix is the one surface that carries the rule — delete it and the principle degrades to prose.

coreThree.title: The task packet
coreThree.ezx: The packet is where the whole process physically converges: the model's data, the plan's scope, the ratified contract anchors, the provenance manifest, and the acceptance inventories all meet in one self-contained, machine-checkable unit of work.

findings.summary: The new-semantic-decision rule stated absolutely; the loop-economics STOPs are a second stop family needing no decision.
Machine-checkable acceptance is necessary, not sufficient: a first-of-a-kind packet is human-approved at any trust stage.
The plan section names ONE commit exception at this head; the instrument-landing second is defined in the packet template and its plan-side text is uncommitted.
The per-chapter packet table is the later form: it starts at plan §6.7, and chapter 3 runs with no task packets.
Source-first is the flow, not an absolute: a direct HTML edit is the named exception, provided re-extraction follows.
The four-role relay is the ch13 hand-over's own choreography, not the general staffing model for heavy work.
A superseded draft transfers its realization obligation to its successor, which must itself stand realized at the close.
The arm-hiding PATH rebuild has a declared opt-out via one documented environment flag.
The coverage checker's inputs do not include the plan; the false `G4 consumes A5` edge dropped.
The IC/PI mapping is procedure-enforced at intake: neither the coverage checker nor the ADR check parses `IC-*`/`PI-*`.
The edge vocabulary reserves `derives-from` for principles and offers no artifact→artifact generation edge; the ledger expresses the relation as `M8 produces A3` and records the gap here.
The scoped, expiring carve-out is not a supersession; the edges were already dropped at the 2026-07-28 fold.

`G6 enforces A6` is defensible under the prompt's own definition: the lint enforces the rules ADRs declare, while G7 validates the ADR document form; both edges are true of different aspects of the same form.
